intro: To ask for something politely, English uses questions with could or would rather than the imperative: “Could you help me?”. Choosing the right level of politeness is essential at work, in shops and with people you don't know.
objectifs: Ask someone to do something with Can / Could / Would you + base verb.
Ask for permission for yourself with Can / Could / May I…?
Use “Would you mind + -ing?” and understand the answers.
Accept or refuse a request politely.

sections.titre: Asking someone to do something: Can / Could / Would you…?
texte: To ask someone to do something, ask a question with a modal + you + base verb. The more “distant” the form, the more polite it sounds.
Here, “could” is not a past form: it is simply more polite. Put “please” after you or at the end of the sentence.

lignes: Could you close the window, please?
Would you mind waiting a moment?
very polite, for a big favour
Could you possibly lend me your car?

sections.titre: Asking for permission: Can / Could / May I…?
texte: When you ask for something for yourself (permission to do something), the subject is I: Can I…?, Could I…?, May I…? (more formal).
“Could I have…?” is the perfect phrase to order or ask for something: “Could I have the bill, please?”. “Can I get…?” is common in American English in cafés, but it is more informal.
exemples: Could I have a glass of water, please?

sections.titre: Would you mind…?: be careful with the answers
texte: “Would you mind + verb-ing?” means “Is it a problem for you to…?”. The verb after mind is always in the -ing form.
Trap: to say yes (to agree to help), you answer with a negative: “No, not at all.” / “Of course not.” (= it's no problem for me). Answering “Yes” would mean “yes, it is a problem”.
exemples: Would you mind opening the door? — No, not at all.
“No” here = I'm happy to do it.
Would you mind speaking more slowly?
Would you mind if I sat here? — Of course not. Go ahead.

texte: To accept, use short, friendly answers: Sure. / Of course. / Yes, no problem. / Certainly (more formal). We don't usually answer a request with “Yes, I could”.
To refuse, say sorry and give a reason: “I'm sorry, but…”, “I'm afraid I can't…”. “I'm afraid” here means “I'm sorry to say”, not “I'm scared”.

lignes: I'm sorry, I can't. I'm in a hurry.
I'm afraid I can't. I'm using it right now.
I'd love to, but I'm busy tonight.

texte: “Would you like…?” (lesson 34) is an offer or invitation: you offer something to someone. “Would you…?” is a request: you ask someone to do something.
An imperative alone (“Close the door.”) can sound rude in English, especially with a stranger. “Please” helps, but a question with could is much more natural.

formule: Can / Could / Would you + base …? · Would you mind + verb-ing …? · Can / Could / May I + base …?
prononciation: “Could you” often sounds like /ˈkʊdʒuː/: d + y join to make /dʒ/; the same with “Would you” /ˈwʊdʒuː/.
“could” /kʊd/ and “would” /wʊd/: the l is silent; “would” sounds like “wood”.
Intonation makes you polite: a voice that rises gently at the end sounds polite; a flat or falling voice can sound like an order.
“please” is /pliːz/, with a z sound at the end; it is often stressed at the end of the sentence.
erreurs: Could you to help me?
Could you help me?
No to after could / would.
Would you mind to open the window?
Would you mind opening the window?
After mind: verb-ing.
Would you mind helping me? — Yes, of course!
Would you mind helping me? — No, not at all! / Of course not!
To agree to “Would you mind…?”, answer with a negative.
Can you give me the bill?
Could I have the bill, please?
More polite and natural in a restaurant: Could I have…?
Please, could you repeat?
Could you repeat that, please?
please usually goes at the end or after you; repeat usually needs an object (that).
Could you help me? — Yes, I could.
Could you help me? — Sure. / Of course.
Don't answer a request with “I could”.
I have fear I can't come.
I'm afraid I can't come.
“I'm sorry to say” = I'm afraid.

dialogue.contexte: At a hotel reception desk in Quebec City. Mr Ndiaye has just arrived after a long trip from Dakar.
lignes: Good evening, sir. How can I help you?
Good evening. I have a reservation. Could you check it, please? The name is Ndiaye.
Of course. Would you mind spelling your name?
Thank you. Here's your key. Room 412.
Thanks. Could I have a wake-up call at six, please?
Could I have…? for a service.
Certainly. Would you like some help with your bags?
Certainly = formal yes; Would you like = an offer.
That would be great. Could you also tell me where I can eat tonight?
Accepting an offer, then a request.
I'm afraid the restaurant is closed, but there's a nice café across the street.
I'm afraid = I'm sorry to say.

mots: Could you do me a favour?
something kind you do to help someone (US: favor)
to feel annoyed or worried about something
Could you lend me a pen?
to give something to someone for a short time
to take something from someone for a short time
to say the letters of a word in order
I'm afraid I can't help you.
It's more polite to say “could you”.
the act of asking for something politely

exercices.consigne: Write the best request for each situation: Can you…? (friend) or Could you…? / Would you mind…? (stranger, work).
items: To your brother: pass you the remote control.
Can you pass me the remote?
To a stranger on the train: turn their music down.
Could you turn your music down, please? / Would you mind turning your music down?
To your manager: read your report.
Could you read my report, please? / Would you mind reading my report?
To a friend: wait for you for five minutes.
Can you wait for me for five minutes?

exercices.consigne: Change the request to Would you mind…?
items: Could you close the door?
Would you mind closing the door?
Could you speak more slowly?
Would you mind speaking more slowly?
Could you send me the file?
Would you mind sending me the file?
Could you move your car?
Would you mind moving your car?

exercices.consigne: Write a polite request with Could I…? or May I…?
items: You want the bill in a restaurant.
Could I have the bill, please?
You want to use the toilet at someone's house.
Could I use your bathroom, please? / May I use your toilet?
You want to borrow a colleague's pen.
Could I borrow your pen?
You want to enter your teacher's office.
May I come in?

exercices.consigne: Answer politely (✓ accept, ✗ refuse with a reason).
items: Would you mind opening the window? (✓)
No, not at all. / Of course not.
Could you help me with my bags? (✓)
Sure! / Of course.
Could you lend me your car tonight? (✗)
I'm sorry, I can't. I need it tonight. / I'm afraid I can't. I'm using it.

exercices.consigne: Each sentence has one mistake. Write it correctly.
items: Could you to call me back?
Could you call me back?
Would you mind to wait here?
Would you mind waiting here?
Can I to sit here?
Can I sit here?
Would you mind helping me? — Yes, sure!
Would you mind helping me? — No, not at all! / Of course not!

exercices.consigne: You are at an office reception or in a shop. Write a short exchange of four or five lines with at least three different polite requests.
items: Model answer

Me: Good morning. Could you tell me where the passport office is, please? — Clerk: Of course. It's on the second floor. — Me: Thank you. Would you mind giving me a form? — Clerk: Not at all. Here you are. — Me: Could I borrow a pen too? — Clerk: Certainly.

a_retenir: Asking someone: Can you…? (informal) → Could / Would you…? (polite) → Would you mind + -ing? (very polite).
Asking for yourself: Can / Could / May I…?; Could I have…, please?
Would you mind…? → to agree: No, not at all / Of course not.
Refusing politely: I'm sorry, but… / I'm afraid I can't…
Here, could is not past; and Would you like…? is an offer, not a request.
